history.title: Crew Launch Week 1: Norms We Can Name and Keep

data.body:
Crew slot: 40 minutes. HOWL: Respect. "I am a respectful member of the King community."

This week your Crew decides how it wants to treat each other, and writes it down in words you can check.

1. Read **Norms We Can Name and Keep** (10 minutes, together or on your own).
2. Learn the words in the **Glossary**, then win the **Word Scramble**.
3. Keep the **Rule or Norm?** chart open while you work.
4. Sort the cards in **Rule, Norm, or Just Polite?**
5. Take the short quiz. It asks what makes a norm a norm.
6. Open the SEL Hub from Learning Tools and choose [Crew Protocols](#sel-hub/crewProtocols?station=sel_station_crew_launch_norms). Plan one protocol your Crew will use this week, with a way to pass.
7. Use the **Sentence Frames** to draft two norms for your Crew.
8. Lock the idea in with **Remember the Three Parts**.
9. Finish with the **Decide Challenge: Our Crew Norms**, where the Crew votes on its top four.

Your commitment: this week, notice one moment in any class where you kept a Crew norm without being reminded. Bring it back to Crew. 🤝

Clicking a tool link above also starts your Crew station for this week, so the time you spend in the tools and the self-check stay together in one place. It stays active until you exit it, so come back later in the week to mark the self-check. You can find it again under SEL Stations in the History panel. 📌

history.title: Norms We Can Name and Keep
history.data:
## Norms We Can Name and Keep

**HOWL: "I am a respectful member of the King community."**

A **Crew** is a small group of people who agree to look out for each other. That agreement does not happen by accident. It happens when the group names, out loud, how it wants to treat each other, and then keeps checking whether it is doing that. Those named agreements are called **norms**.

A norm is not a **rule** from a poster. A rule is something an adult gives you. A norm is something the group chooses together and can explain in its own words. "Be respectful" is a rule. "We wait until someone finishes before we answer" is a norm, because you can see it happening or not happening.

Here is a moment from a fictional Crew. On the second day, Amara starts to share about her weekend and two people begin a side conversation. Amara stops mid-sentence. Nobody is trying to be mean. But the Crew has not yet decided what it does when someone is talking. The Crew leader, Mr. Okafor, does not lecture. He asks, "What do we want to happen when someone is sharing?" The group builds a norm together: one voice at a time, and a small hand **signal** if you need to add something. The next day, when the side talk starts again, a student taps the signal. The talking stops. Nobody had to be told.

Good norms have three parts. They are **specific**, so you can tell whether they happened. They are **shared**, so everyone helped choose them. And they are **revisited**, so the group can change them when they stop working. A norm that nobody remembers is not a norm. It is a poster.

Norms protect **participation**, too. Some people speak easily. Some need time to think. Some would rather write or draw than talk. A Crew that only rewards fast talkers is not a respectful Crew, even if everyone is being polite. So strong norms include a way to **pass**, a way to think first, and a way to join later. A pass is not a refusal. It is a signal that you are still part of the circle.

Working **cooperatively** is the first respect behavior in the King **HOWLs**. Cooperation is not the same as agreeing. It means you can disagree and still keep the norms. It means the group's work gets done and nobody got run over while it happened.

This week, your Crew will name its norms. The test of a norm is not whether it sounds nice. The test is whether you can catch yourself keeping it on Thursday.

history.title: What Makes a Norm a Norm?

questions.question: A Crew writes "Be respectful" on its poster. Why is this not yet a norm?
options: Because respect is not important in a Crew
Because you cannot see whether it happened or not
Because it was written on a poster instead of a screen
Because it was chosen by students and not a teacher
questions.correctAnswer: Because you cannot see whether it happened or not

questions.question: In the reading, what did Mr. Okafor do when side talk interrupted Amara?
options: He asked the group what should happen when someone shares
He moved the two students to a different Crew for a week
He told the group the rule about talking and moved on
He asked Amara to speak louder so everyone could hear
questions.correctAnswer: He asked the group what should happen when someone shares

questions.question: A student says "pass" during a share round. What does that mean in a Crew with strong norms?
options: The student is refusing to be part of the Crew today
The student is in trouble and the leader will follow up
The student is still part of the circle, just not speaking this turn
The student has to share twice in the next round to make up for it
questions.correctAnswer: The student is still part of the circle, just not speaking this turn

questions.question: Which statement about cooperation matches the reading?
options: Cooperating means agreeing with the group so the work gets done
Cooperating means the loudest person makes the decision quickly
Cooperating means keeping quiet so that there is no disagreement
Cooperating means you can disagree and still keep the norms
questions.correctAnswer: Cooperating means you can disagree and still keep the norms

questions.question: A norm has been on the wall since September and nobody remembers it. What does the reading say the Crew should do?
options: Replace it with a rule from the handbook so it carries weight
Revisit it as a group and change it if it stopped working
Leave it up, because norms should never be changed once set
Have the Crew leader decide privately whether to keep it or not
questions.correctAnswer: Revisit it as a group and change it if it stopped working

questions.question: Rewrite "Be a good listener" so that it passes the specific part of the three-part test.
questions.expectedAnswer: Any visible action, for example: We wait until the speaker finishes before we respond, or We look at the person who is sharing.

reflections.text: Which of your Crew norms would be easiest for you to keep on a hard day? Which would be hardest? Why?

data.rubric:
| Criteria | 1 - Starting | 3 - Getting There | 5 - Crew Ready |
|---|---|---|---|
| Specific | Sounds nice but cannot be seen | Names one visible action | Names the action and what it looks like when it fails |
| Shared | Written alone | Discussed with a partner | Discussed by the Crew and voted on |
| Protects participation | No way to pass or think | Includes a pass or think time | Includes pass, think time, and a way to join later |

data.question: What is Crew, anyway?
data.answer: Crew is your school's word for a small group of students and one adult who meet regularly to check in, set goals, and work through hard things together. It comes from EL Education, the school model King has used since 1992, and from an old idea about ships: everyone on board is crew, not a passenger. Read more on [King's EL page](https://king.portlandschools.org/about/learning-models) or [EL Education's Crew page](https://www.eleducation.org/crew).

data.question: What is a HOWL?
data.answer: A Habit of Work and Learning. Your school scores three of them, apart from your academic grades: Respect ("I am a respectful member of the King community"), Responsibility ("I take responsibility for my success as a learner"), and Perseverance ("I persevere to produce high quality work"). Teachers score them; Crew is where you practice them. The statements are on [King's grading guide](https://king.portlandschools.org/families/handbook/handbook-interior/~board/king-student-family-handbook/post/grading-guide).

data.question: What if someone keeps breaking a norm?
data.answer: First, the Crew revisits it. Sometimes the norm is unclear or does not fit. If it is clear and still broken, the Crew leader handles it privately. Norms are not a reason to call someone out in the circle.

data.question: Can we change a norm in the middle of the year?
data.answer: Yes. That is the "revisited" part. Norms that cannot change stop being the group's and start being a poster.

data.question: Is passing a way to get out of Crew?
data.answer: No. Passing means you are choosing not to speak this turn. You are still listening and still in the circle. Passing every single time is worth a private conversation with your Crew leader, not a comment from the group.

data.question: Do we need a norm for everything?
data.answer: No. Four or five that the Crew actually remembers beat fifteen that nobody does.

data.question: How is this connected to my HOWL grade?
data.answer: The Respect HOWL says you work cooperatively with others. Keeping a norm in a class where nobody is reminding you is what that looks like. Your teachers score HOWLs; Crew is where you practice them.

cards.target: The three parts of a good norm: specific, shared, revisited
essentialFacts: They are specific, so you can tell whether they happened.
They are shared, so everyone helped choose them.
They are revisited, so the group can change them when they stop working.
cards.aiExample: S-S-R: See it, Share it, Revisit it. If you can See it happen, everyone Shared in choosing it, and you Revisit it when it fails, it is a norm.
cards.mapping: See stands for specific (you can see it happen). Share stands for shared (chosen together). Revisit stands for revisited (checked and changed).
cards.scaffoldStarter: S is for ____. S is for ____. R is for ____.
scaffoldSteps: Write the three words from the reading.
Pick one action verb for each.
Say the three verbs in order out loud.
coachPrompts: Which of the three parts is missing from "Be nice"?
cards.studentPrompt: Make your own three-letter hook for specific, shared, revisited.
cards.reasoningPrompt: How does your hook help you decide whether a sentence on the wall is a norm or a poster?

hookFact.text: A norm that nobody remembers is not a norm. It is a poster.
hookFact.sourceTitle: Norms We Can Name and Keep (this lesson)

cards.target: A pass is not a refusal; it is a signal that you are still in the circle
essentialFacts: A pass is not a refusal.
It is a signal that you are still part of the circle.
cards.aiExample: PASS = still PRESENT. The two words start the same way. Passing keeps you present; it just skips your turn to talk.
cards.mapping: Pass links to present through the shared first letter, so the word itself reminds you that passing does not remove you from the circle.
scaffoldSteps: Find a word that means "still here" that starts the same way.
Say them together as a pair.
coachPrompts: What would a Crew look like where passing felt like being in trouble?
cards.studentPrompt: Make your own word pair for pass.
cards.reasoningPrompt: How does your pair help you treat a classmate who passes?

history.title: Decide Challenge: Our Crew Norms

data.title: Our Crew Norms
data.instructions: Your Crew has a list of draft norms from the sentence frames. Decide together which four to adopt for the trimester, using the three-part test, and write them so a new Crew member could keep them on day one.
data.fitReason: The HOWL behavior is working cooperatively with others. Choosing norms as a group is cooperation in practice: the Crew has to disagree, test each draft against the three parts, and still reach a decision everyone can keep.

brief.context: Your Crew has eight to twelve draft norms written by different members. Some overlap. Some are really rules. Some cannot be checked. The Crew can carry four into the trimester.
brief.audience: Your own Crew, and a student who joins King mid-year and reads the norms on their first day
brief.drivingQuestion: Which four norms should our Crew adopt, and how do we know each one passes the three-part test?
brief.seedDirection: Before voting, test each draft: can you see it happen, did the group help choose it, and could you revisit it? Cut or rewrite anything that fails, then vote.
lockedLessonFacts: A norm is an agreement the group chooses together and can explain in its own words.
Good norms are specific, shared, and revisited.
Strong norms include a way to pass, a way to think first, and a way to join later.
Cooperation is not the same as agreeing; you can disagree and still keep the norms.
openQuestions: Which drafts are really rules from an adult?
Which two drafts say the same thing and can be merged?
stakeholders: Quiet Crew members who need think time
criteria: Each adopted norm passes all three parts of the test
At least one norm protects participation with a pass or think time
The final four are written in words a new student could keep on day one
The decision record shows one disagreement and how the Crew settled it
Uses at least three glossary words in the record
constraints: Every Crew member votes or passes
The Crew sets a revisit date within four weeks
brief.deliverable: A one-page Crew norms card with four norms, the pass signal, and the revisit date, plus a short decision record of what was cut and why.

parallelExample.context: A fictional Crew had a draft that said "Be supportive."
parallelExample.move: They tested it: nobody could say what it looked like. One member rewrote it as "When someone shares something hard, we respond before we change the subject." It passed the test and got the most votes.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: It shows that a vague draft is not thrown out; it is made specific so the Crew can catch itself keeping it.

supports.frameStarter: We adopted "____" because it is specific (we can see ____), shared (____ helped write it), and we will revisit it on ____.
coachPrompts: Which norm would a new student have the hardest time understanding?
Is there a norm on your list that only works for people who like to talk?

data.coachHint: If the Crew gets stuck on wording, ask what it would look like on video. If you could not point to it on video, it is not specific yet.
